name: Figma
tagline: Collaborative browser-based design and prototyping tool

pricing.notes: Official pricing/help checked 2026-07-30; Professional Full seat listed at $20/month monthly and $16/month annually.

verdictSummary: You can make a small drawing/prototyping tool, but Figma's moat is real-time multiplayer editing, plugin ecosystem, design-system workflows, performance, and enterprise trust.
coreLoopDIY: Build a simple canvas editor with rectangles/text/components and export, but expect it to be a toy compared with Figma.
whatYouLose: your team, who are all on Figma
ten years of canvas performance engineering
whyPeopleStillPay: They pay because entire product/design teams coordinate inside the file, not because drawing rectangles is hard.

priorArt.name: Penpot
priorArt.desc: open-source design tool — the serious alternative

notes: The credibility entry. Figma's value is multiplayer CRDTs, a decade of canvas engineering, and everyone else being on it. You can't one-shot a moat — and network effects are the strongest moat there is.
prompt:
Honest answer: don't. Figma's core value is multiplayer editing on a
high-performance canvas plus the fact that your whole team already lives there.
A one-shot clone gives you a worse Excalidraw and none of the network.

If what you actually need is single-player vector editing, run Penpot
(open source, self-hostable) or Excalidraw instead · links in prior art.

If you still want to scratch the itch, here's the weekend version:

- A canvas editor: rectangles, ellipses, text, and frames; select, move,
  resize with handles; fill/stroke/corner-radius controls in a right panel.
- Layers list with drag-reorder, and export of the selection as SVG and PNG.
- Local-first: documents persist to IndexedDB, import/export as JSON.
- Vanilla JS or Svelte on a single canvas element; no backend at all.

What you will NOT have: multiplayer, comments, components, auto-layout,
plugins, or anyone to collaborate with. That gap is the product.
